title: Finite and countable sets: counting, enumeration, and examples

based_on.title: B1.2 Set Theory
based_on.pages: 43 (finite-subset argument in the proof of Theorem 10.2(ii))

summary: Count finite sets, enumerate integers and rationals, and prove that subsets, images, finite unions, and finite products of countable sets are countable.
abstract: There are infinitely many rational numbers between any two different rationals, yet every rational can be put on a single list. A set is countable when its elements can be listed, using a finite list or positions indexed by the natural numbers. The integers, pairs of natural numbers, and finite subsets of a countable set all have this property. Different fractions can describe the same rational number, but discarding repetitions gives a list in which every rational appears exactly once.
